title: Twice the razzle dazzle!! #broadway #musicaltheatre #funfact #chicago...
transcript: Why was the Broadway revival of Chicago playing in two different theatres at the same time, less than a mile apart, for one week only in 2016? Well, I'll tell you! so welcome to another episode of Overthinking Theatre Throwback, where I do retrospectives on recent theatre history. First, I just wanna emphasize how weird and rare of a situation this is for a show that's not in the public domain. Because if you don't know, even if people in charge of licensing allowed two productions in the same city at the same time, which they very rarely do, You still would not expect to see two of the same production. So what happened here? Well, I don't claim to know the details of the contracts and the licensing agreement, but whatever deal they struck, they clearly wanted to make an exception for some very special guests, Because in July of 2016, the Lincoln Center Festival played host to a very rare New York appearance from the iconic Takarazuka Revue, an incredibly popular theatre company in Japan that often performs very well known works, but always with all female casts. There's a lot of fascinating backstory with the Takarazuka Revue, but to quickly summarize, it was founded in 1913 by a railway company trying to increase tourism to the city of Takarazuka. And that's where they still operate, But their success has also allowed them to tour all around the world. But they rarely come to the U S. And even more rarely come to New York. This run in 2016 was their first time in New York in 24 years, and now is still the most recent to date. And for their version of Chicago, which marked Takarazuka's Centennial anniversary, they got permission to recreate Walter Bobbie’s famous Broadway revival staging, the same that was and still is playing on Broadway since 1996. The amusing overlap didn't go unnoticed. They even had a press event where the two casts met each other. And as a slight side note, another extremely rare case of this happening was in 1996 when the Broadway revival of Grease was still running, when their national tour played a weekend engagement at City Center. Funny enough, those were the same producers as Chicago on Broadway, so I guess if anyone was gonna let an exception like this happen, it would be the Weisslers. However, while Takarazuka’s Chicago was the same physical production that was playing on Broadway, there were still three key differences. (1) it was performed in Japanese, obviously. (2) per Takarazuka tradition, it was an all female cast. Although they did break from that tradition slightly by having Mary Sunshine still played by a man, making that reveal probably even more impactful than it is in the Broadway production. But (3), and maybe most significant of all, the performance of Chicago was followed immediately by the Takarazuka encore, basically a bonus performance with almost Vegas-style glitz and glamor, where they performed a 20 minute set Of assorted songs not from the show. Because of these differences, I'm never sure what to say when people ask me the last time I saw this revival. Like, I haven't seen it since 2007, except for the one time I saw it in 2016. But I would venture that I had a pretty different experience from the people who saw it on Broadway that same week.
classificationReason: This is an 'Overthinking Theatre Throwback' retrospective explaining why the Broadway revival of Chicago played in two different theatres simultaneously in 2016 (due to a Takarazuka Revue guest engagement). It is historical commentary about a past licensing oddity, not a first-hand review of the current production.
